title: Review: Factors affecting membrane permeability; Specific immune response: antigens and lymphocytes; Vaccination and herd immunity; Non-specific defences; Antibodies, primary/secondary responses and immunity types
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for AQA A-level Biology (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: IM05#t3 term and clue written for the game; IM05#t2 term and clue written for the game; IM02#t1 term and clue written for the game; IM05#t1 term and clue written for the game. Questions: IM02#N.9, IM03#N.14, IM04#N.3, IM05#N.4, MB05#N.8, IM02#N.11, IM03#N.4, IM04#N.9, IM05#N.13, IM02#N.13, IM03#N.2, IM05#N.11b. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Secondary response
items.clue: Fast reaction that meets a later infection after an earlier exposure to the antigen.

items.label: Primary response
items.clue: First reaction to an antigen: plasma cells, antibodies and memory cells are produced.

items.label: Phagocyte
items.clue: Defensive cell that recognises foreign molecules, then engulfs and digests the pathogen.

items.label: Vaccine
items.clue: Contains antigens, or mRNA or DNA coding for one, and triggers protection without disease.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes the innate immune system from the adaptive immune system?

options.text: Both systems build up a memory of the pathogens they meet, but the innate system does so faster because it does not need to be specific to each one.
The innate system is the specific one, with each phagocyte recognising just a single type of pathogen, while the lymphocytes respond to broad categories of pathogen.
The innate system responds to broad categories of pathogen and does not change during life; the adaptive system is specific and builds a memory of pathogens.
The adaptive system responds faster than the innate system on first exposure to a pathogen, because a specific response is a more efficient response.

questions.explanation: The innate response (including phagocytes) is the same on every exposure, whereas the adaptive response is specific to particular pathogens and becomes more effective because a memory of pathogens encountered is retained.

questions.stem: A child is born with no T lymphocytes. Her B lymphocytes are normal in number and type. Why does she make very little antibody against most pathogens?

options.text: T lymphocytes normally secrete most of the body's antibodies, so without them little antibody is made.
B cells need T cells to show them the antigen's shape, so that they can then design an antibody to fit it.
This should not happen: a B cell starts making antibody as soon as it binds its antigen.
B cells that bind antigen are not activated without T helper cells, so no plasma cells form.

questions.stem: Antibodies against measles and antibodies against tetanus toxin are compared. Which part of the molecule differs between them?

options.text: The disulfide bridges, which create a different binding site in each antibody.
The constant region, which is shaped to fit the antigen.
The variable region, which forms the antigen-binding site.
The number of polypeptide chains, which depends on the size of the antigen.

questions.explanation: Different amino acid sequences in the variable regions give different binding sites, each complementary to its own antigen.

questions.stem: For measles, transmission in a population is greatly impeded once about 95% of people are immune. A community's vaccination coverage falls from 96% to 85%. Which statement correctly describes a consequence?

options.text: The unvaccinated people remain immune too, because herd immunity continues to protect the whole population permanently once it has been reached.
Only the people who chose not to be vaccinated are affected, because each person's vaccination status affects only their own risk of infection.
There is no consequence, because measles was eliminated from the community while coverage was above 95% and so cannot return.
People who are not immune, including those who cannot be vaccinated, are at greater risk because chains of transmission are no longer broken.

questions.stem: A student makes a 1-in-10 dilution series: each step transfers 1.0 cm³ of the previous solution into 9.0 cm³ of distilled water. What is the concentration in the third diluted tube, as a fraction of the stock?
questions.explanation: Each step is 1.0 cm³ in a total of 10.0 cm³: ×1/10. Three steps: (1/10)³ = 1/1000.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes how a phagocyte destroys a bacterium?

options.text: It secretes enzymes from its lysosomes onto the bacterium, digesting it outside the cell, and then absorbs the soluble products.
It engulfs the bacterium by endocytosis and then digests it inside the cell, using the enzymes from its lysosomes.
It lets the bacterium pass straight through its plasma membrane into the cytoplasm, where cytoplasmic enzymes break it down.
It binds to the bacterium using a receptor specific to that strain and holds it until lymphocytes arrive to destroy it.

questions.explanation: Phagocytes recognise pathogens, engulf them by endocytosis so that the pathogen is enclosed in a vesicle, and digest them using enzymes from lysosomes that fuse with the vesicle.

questions.stem: Which statement about B-lymphocytes and antibodies is correct?

options.text: Each B-lymphocyte examines the antigen it meets and then adjusts the shape of the antibody it makes so that it fits the antigen.
Helper T-cells and B-lymphocytes both secrete antibodies, which is why they are said to cooperate in producing them.
A person has a very large number of different B-lymphocytes, and each of them makes a single specific type of antibody.
B-lymphocytes are found only in the blood; lymph nodes contain trapped pathogens but no lymphocytes at all.

questions.explanation: The diversity of B-cells, not any tailoring by an individual cell, is what allows a specific response to almost any antigen.

questions.stem: What is the basis of a person's immunity to a disease that they have previously had?

options.text: Memory cells that are specific to the pathogen survive long-term and can make the antibodies that are needed.
Antibodies made during the first infection remain in the blood at a protective level for the rest of the person's life.
Memory cells are plasma cells that keep on secreting the antibody at a low rate for many years after the infection.
Phagocytes of the innate immune system learned to recognise the pathogen during the first infection and now destroy it faster.

questions.explanation: Immunity is the ability to eliminate an infectious disease from the body. It is due to the long-term survival of lymphocytes that are capable of making the specific antibodies needed: memory cells.

questions.stem: A news article reports a newly published study claiming that a vaccine causes a rare side effect, before other scientists have evaluated the study. Which response shows the best understanding of how science works?

options.text: Accept the claim as established, because a study that has been published in a scientific journal has been proven to be correct.
Conclude that the vaccine is unsafe, because a vaccine that is genuinely safe would carry no risk of side effects of any kind.
Treat the claim as provisional until other scientists have evaluated the study; vaccine risks are minimal but not nil.
Dismiss the claim without reading it, because vaccines are tested so rigorously that a side effect of any kind is impossible.

questions.stem: In a phagocyte, the lysosomes cannot fuse with phagosomes, but every other step works normally. What happens to a bacterium that meets this phagocyte?

options.text: It is engulfed, then digested in the cytoplasm by enzymes released from the phagosome.
It is digested outside the cell instead, by lysosomal enzymes secreted onto it.
It is not engulfed, because engulfing depends on lysosomes.
It is engulfed but survives inside the phagosome, as no enzymes reach it.

questions.explanation: Engulfing and digesting are separate steps. Without fusion, the enzymes never reach the bacterium.

questions.stem: Which statement about antigens is correct?

options.text: Antigens are proteins made by lymphocytes that bind to pathogens and mark them for destruction by the phagocytes.
Most antigens are glycoproteins or other proteins, usually located on the outer surface of a pathogen.
Antigens are toxins released by a pathogen into the blood, and it is these toxins that the antibodies must neutralise.
Antigens are found only on pathogens; molecules on the surface of human cells do not act as antigens.

questions.explanation: Antigens are recognition molecules that trigger antibody production. Most are glycoproteins or other proteins on the outer surfaces of pathogens, where the immune system can recognise them.

questions.stem: Which conclusion is valid from the trial data in N.10?

options.text: In this trial, vaccinated adults had about 95% fewer cases of symptomatic COVID-19 than those given the placebo.
The vaccine protects 95% of people for life.
The vaccine caused COVID-19 in the 8 vaccinated people who became ill.
Only 8 of 18 198 vaccinated people became ill, so the vaccine is 99.96% effective.

questions.explanation: Efficacy compares the two groups' risk: (0.44 − 8.84) ÷ 8.84 × 100 = −95%.
